# The Strange Necessity of Silence

There is a moment, usually late at night, when the world finally stops moving. Not the metaphorical kind of stop — not the Zen master's suggestion to "stop and smell the roses" — but an actual, physical cessation of noise. The traffic thins. The neighbors go to bed. The refrigerator's hum becomes not a background disturbance but the loudest thing in the room. And in that moment, you become aware of yourself in a way that daytime rarely permits.

I think about silence more than I should. Or rather, I think about its absence more than I should, which amounts to the same thing. We live in a world engineered for sound. Every algorithm that governs your phone, your social media feed, your streaming service, is designed to fill the void that would otherwise exist. The void terrifies us — or more precisely, the technology industry has concluded that the void terrifies us, and so it fills it on our behalf, whether we asked for it or not.

A musician I once knew told me that silence is not the absence of music but the medium in which music exists. Without it, you wouldn't hear a note. I always thought that was a little too neat, a little too Instagram-ready for my taste, but the longer I've lived, the more I've found it true in ways that extend far beyond music.

---

**The Problem With Always Having Something To Say**

We have arrived at an interesting historical moment. For most of human history, information was scarce. You knew what your neighbor knew. Knowledge was passed orally, recorded by scribes, limited to what could be carried on a ship or carried in a head. Then printing made information abundant. Then radio, then television, then the internet made it infinite. Now we live in an age where information is so abundant that it has become meaningless — or rather, where the abundance itself is a kind of absence. A whiteout. You can find an answer to any question in seconds, but the experience of not knowing, of sitting with a question without reaching for your phone, has become almost unbearable for many of us.

There's something profoundly alien about a culture that cannot tolerate not knowing. I once watched a friend mid-conversation with his phone in his hand, the screen black but the thumb hovering, ready. He wasn't checking anything. He was just... holding it, the way a smoker holds a cigarette between fingers, the way a drowning person reaches for something — anything — that might be solid. The phone was a talisman against the possibility that the conversation might enter a territory where neither of us had words yet.

And here's the thing: those territories — those stretches of silence in conversation where the unformed thought is hovering just out of reach — are where the most interesting things happen. When you let a thought finish developing before you speak it, it is invariably different from the thought you blurted out at the first flicker of recognition. Silence gives ideas time to grow teeth.

This is why I've always been suspicious of people who talk constantly, not because loudness offends me, but because their words feel rehearsed. They are running on a script, and the script exists to prevent the silence that might reveal that there's no one home behind the words. I don't mean that cruelly. I mean it the way you might observe a person who is afraid of heights building elaborate arguments about why they don't want to go to the edge. The avoidance tells you more about their interior life than anything they've actually said.

---

**Silence as a Political Act**

But silence isn't merely personal. It has always been political, and its politics have only intensified in the age of digital performance.

Consider the way public discourse works now. You are expected to have an opinion on everything — every tragedy, every controversy, every cultural moment — and you are expected to express that opinion immediately, in public, in a format that can be liked or shared or ratioed. If you remain silent, your silence is itself interpreted as a statement. Not speaking becomes a form of speaking, and so the demand for speech metastasizes into a demand for total speech, speech without rest, speech without thinking.

There was a period a few years ago when I noticed that I couldn't read the news without feeling an obligation to publicly respond to it. Not because I had something original to say — I rarely did — but because staying silent felt like complicity. Like neutrality in the face of horror. And maybe sometimes it was. But more often, it was just my brain trying to satisfy an artificial demand. I was performing outrage, performing care, performing the identity of a person who cares, and the performance was exhausting in a way that left no room for actually caring.

The problem is that genuine caring — the kind that changes something — requires depth, and depth requires time, and time requires the willingness to be silent for a long while before speaking. You cannot care well if you care quickly. You cannot grieve well if you must document your grief in real time for an audience of followers. You cannot love well if your understanding of love is mediated through a feed that shows you only the highlights of other people's love, stripped of all context, all duration, all boredom, all silence.

I think about the writers I admire most, and I notice that many of them were comfortable with silence — or at least, comfortable with the anxiety of silence, which is not the same thing but is the next best thing. Thomas Bernhard lived in a farmhouse in Austria and wrote novels that were, essentially, one continuous scream against the moral cowardice of his culture. He didn't need an audience to validate the scream before it was finished. Kafka wrote to a few friends and a girlfriend and sent much of his work to be burned after his death. We are lucky he overrode the instruction, but the fact that it occurred to him tells you something about the relationship between creativity and indifference to reception.

---

**The Body Knows Silence Before the Mind Does**

Here is something I've learned about silence that no one told me when I was young: your body registers it before your mind does. If you sit in a quiet room for twenty minutes — genuinely quiet, no music, no podcast, no scrolling — something shifts. Your breathing slows. Your shoulders drop. Your thoughts, which had been racing along a track at high speed, begin to meander, to double back, to sometimes stop altogether. And in that stopping, a kind of information arrives that is not verbal, not even particularly cognitive. It is more like a temperature change. You feel the emotional weather of your own life, and often the forecast is not what you expected.

I spent a year living alone in a small town where I knew almost nobody. It was, by any rational measure, a failure — a year of underemployment and awkward social encounters and eating dinner at the kitchen table while a cat I'd inherited from the previous tenant judged me from across the room. But I also spent that year in more silence than I had ever experienced, and it rewired something in me. Not in a dramatic, transformative way — I didn't emerge from my hermitage with answers to the great questions — but in a quiet way. I became less afraid of not knowing. I became less afraid of the gap between questions. I became able to sit with an unfinished thought the way you sit with a simmering pot, trusting that the heat will do its work.

Before that year, silence felt like failure. Like being alone at a party, like having nothing to offer, like falling behind. After that year, silence felt like terrain — sometimes flat and boring, sometimes forested and confusing, but always real, always something to move through rather than flee from.

---

**The Sonic Architecture of Everyday Life**

Let me turn away from the philosophical for a moment and talk about something more concrete: the actual sounds of daily life, and how strange they've become.

We are surrounded by sounds that our ancestors would not have recognized and would likely have found terrifying. The hum of fluorescent lights. The buzz of a cell phone vibrating on a wooden table, a sound so low and rhythmic that it sometimes feels like it's coming from inside your own chest. The whir of a computer fan. The distant, barely perceptible drone of the city itself — a sound so constant that it has become, for most urban dwellers, synonymous with silence. They would hear it only when it stopped, during a blackout or a natural disaster, and then, paradoxically, the silence would feel threatening.

I remember being caught in a power outage during a summer storm when I was in my twenties. The neighborhood went dark and the sound went with it — no air conditioners, no refrigerators, no traffic lights buzzing, no TVs bleeding from every window. And in that silence, for the first time in months, I could hear the rain. Not the rain as a backdrop, not rain-as-ambiance, but rain as individual drops striking individual surfaces — the tin roof over the fire escape, the broad leaf of a magnolia tree, the gutter that someone had failed to clear for years. Each drop had its own tone. The composition was unrepeatable. I stood on my fire escape for twenty minutes, soaking wet, marveling at something I had been hearing without hearing my entire life.

That's what silence does, when it arrives uninvited. It makes you hear what was always there.

---

**Writing as a Negotiation With Silence**

Since this is an essay, it seems fair to talk about writing and silence, because they are locked in a relationship that most writers never fully understand.

Writing, at its core, is an act of emerging from silence into language, and it is always, to some degree, a loss. You have a thought — it exists in your mind with a texture and a color and an emotional resonance that is richer than any sentence you could produce. Then you put it into words, and the words approximate the thought, but they are not the thought. They are a scaffold built around the thought, and the thought, like a building, is visible only through the scaffolding. The scaffolding is not the building. But without the scaffolding, the building cannot be seen at all.

So you are always choosing between two failures: the failure to communicate (silence) and the failure to preserve (language). And you must choose, every time, to fail in the second way, because the first way is not a failure at all but a non-event. The thought dies unshared, and no one, including you, will ever know what it was.

This is why writing is terrifying. Not because of the possibility of rejection or bad reviews or the blank page — those are the terrors people talk about, the performative terrors. The real terror is that you will put the wrong words down, that the scaffolding will be crooked and the building behind it will be invisible, and you'll spend your whole life adding scaffolding without ever building anything.

I think about this every time I sit down to write something. The silence before the first word is the silence of potential, of the thought still intact, still rich with its original meaning. The first word destroys it — not violently, not completely, but destructively, in the way that opening a sealed letter changes the meaning of the letter. From that moment on, you are working with ruins. You are doing your best to build something honest from what remains.

And yet. And yet, the writing happens. The words come. Sometimes they're good, sometimes they're terrible, but the act of translation — from silence to speech, from interior to exterior — remains the most human thing we do. We are the only species that carries its inner life out into the shared world through a deliberate, sustained act of encoding. A whale sings, but it does not write. A bee dances, but it does not compose.

---

**What We Owe the Quiet**

I want to end with a small, practical observation, because I've spent enough time in abstraction.

I think we owe the quiet in our lives more respect than we give it. I think we should protect it the way we protect other scarce resources — with intention, with boundaries, with a willingness to say no to the things that would fill it.

I don't mean this as a lifestyle tip. I don't mean wake up at 5 a.m. and meditate for an hour and journal about your gratitude (though if that works for you, by all means). I mean something simpler. I mean: when you notice that you've been reaching for your phone in a moment of quiet, notice that you've done it. When you turn on music to fill the car ride that was already fine, notice that you've done it. When you feel the instinct to speak in a conversation where neither person has anything to say yet, wait. Wait one more beat. See what arrives.

Something always arrives. It might be a thought. It might be an emotion. It might be a memory you'd forgotten you had, surfacing like a fish breaking the water. Or it might be nothing at all, and the nothing might be the most important thing — the confirmation that you exist even when you're not performing, even when you're not producing, even when no one is watching.

There is a quality of aliveness that only emerges in silence. It's not dramatic. It doesn't lend itself to a post or a thread or a hot take. It's quieter than that. It's the feeling of your own nervous system running at its natural speed, unaccelerated by stimulation, undecayed by panic. It's the feeling of being, rather than doing. And it is available, every day, to anyone willing to stop.

The world will not give it to you. The world is not in the business of giving you quiet. The world is in the business of filling every gap, monetizing every pause, selling you something in the moment between your attention and your attention's next destination. If you want silence, you must take it. You must steal it. You must guard it the way you'd guard a fire in the winter — constantly, defensively, knowing that it will go out if you turn your back for even a moment.

But when you have it — when you finally have it — it gives you back something you didn't know you'd lost: yourself, undisturbed, unedited, unperformed. Your original sound, which is no sound at all, but the space in which every other sound means something.

Sit with that for a while. Don't reach for the phone. Just sit. See what comes.

Something will come. It always does.
